Define the key elements of epipolar geometry (baseline, epipolar plane, epipoles, epipolar lines) and state the epipolar constraint and its usefulness.
risposta: Epipolar geometry relates the two projections of a 3D point seen from two views. The baseline connects the two camera centers; the epipolar plane is defined by the 3D point and both centers; the epipoles are where the baseline meets each image plane (the epipole in one image is the projection of the other camera's center); the epipolar line is the intersection of the epipolar plane with an image plane, and all epipolar lines pass through the epipole. The epipolar constraint says a point x in one image has its correspondence on the epipolar line l' in the other image, because the 3D point lies on the back-projected ray whose projection is l'. This reduces the correspondence search from 2D to a 1D line, greatly simplifying matching (especially for unrectified pairs).

domanda: Derive and explain the essential matrix, listing its properties.
risposta: For calibrated cameras (K known), work in normalized coordinates x=K^{-1} p (which converts pixels to an ideal f=1 camera on the z=1 plane). With R,t transforming the first camera frame to the second, the two optical centers and the 3D point are coplanar, giving the coplanarity condition (x-t)^T (t x x)=0 (the cross product t x x is orthogonal to the epipolar plane). Using the skew-symmetric form [t]_x and substituting the transformation yields x'^T E x = 0 with the essential matrix E=R[t]_x. Properties: it relates points in normalized camera coordinates, has rank 2 (det=0 since [t]_x is rank 2), has 5 DOF (3 rotation + 2 translation direction), and has two equal nonzero singular values. Unlike a homography (point to point), E maps a point to an epipolar line.

domanda: Explain the fundamental matrix, how it relates to the essential matrix, and how the (normalized) 8-point algorithm estimates it.
risposta: The fundamental matrix F generalizes E to uncalibrated cameras, operating directly on pixels: p'^T F p = 0, with F=K'^{-T} E K^{-1}=K'^{-T} [t]_x R K^{-1}. It has rank 2 (det=0), 7 DOF (8 from a projective map minus 1 for rank), maps pixels to epipolar lines, and provides a weak calibration. Ranking: H rank 3 / 8 DOF, F rank 2 / 7 DOF, E rank 2 / 5 DOF; homography is a special case for planar scenes. The 8-point algorithm uses >=8 correspondences (F is up to scale) to solve Af=0 by minimizing ||Af||^2 with ||f||=1 via the smallest eigenvector of A^T A. The basic version is noise-sensitive because A's columns have very different magnitudes; the normalized version first translates points to zero centroid and scales so the mean distance is sqrt(2), runs the 8-point algorithm, enforces rank 2 by zeroing the smallest singular value (SVD), then denormalizes F=T'^T F_hat T.

domanda: Explain linear triangulation, its limitation, and the better non-linear alternative.
risposta: Once the projection matrices P,P' and a correspondence (x,x') are known, triangulation finds the 3D point X. Since x ~ PX and x' ~ P'X are homogeneous, rewrite them with the cross product to drop the unknown scale: x x (PX)=0 and x' x (P'X)=0. Each gives two independent linear equations in X (defined up to scale, so 3 free parameters); stacking both views forms a homogeneous system AX=0 solved by SVD. The limitation is that, due to noise, the back-projected rays generally do not intersect, and the linear SVD solution minimizes an algebraic error rather than the true geometric error. Bundle adjustment, a non-linear optimization, instead minimizes the reprojection error in the images for an accurate 3D estimate.
